newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-ANZ Australia job ads fall 2.9 pct in July.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-ANZ Australia job ads fall 2.9 pct in July.

text.p: The Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd (ANZ) said on Monday its job advertisement series fell by 2.9 percent in July after a 0.8 percent rise in June, but was still up 3.8 percent over the past year.
In trend terms, advertisements rose 0.1 percent in July, compared with a revised 0.7 percent in June. Trend growth has slowed for four consecutive months since peaking at 2.4 percent in March.

"Growth in the demand for labour appears to have eased off slightly over the past few months, even allowing for the distortions caused by the earlier-than-usual occurence of Easter," said ANZ chief economist Saul Eslake.
He noted that in the three months ended July, job ads rose by 3.9 percent in trend terms compared with a 6.0 percent increase in the preceding three months.
"The current level of job advertising continues to be consistent with net new job creation averaging around 13,000 per month over the next few months," said Eslake.
That compared with the average 25,000 a month needed to meet the government's budget target of 2.0 percent employment growth.
Indeed, given the weakness of employment since the May budget reaching the target would require through year growth of at least 3.25 percent, he said.
Eslake noted employment growth in the past few months had been weaker than foreshadowed by the level of job advertising earlier in the year.
He thought this might reflect the apparently sharp rise in the number of discouraged workers who had dropped out of the labour force since late last year.
"This means the measured unemployment rate is not fully capturing the extent of job losses in recent months," he said.

As a result, the model which ANZ used to derive short term employment forecasts from the level of advertisements was probably not fully capturing the impact of corporate and public sector restructuring on the net demand for labour, said Eslake.
"Conversely, when employment does turn around, it may do so more strongly than indicated by the level of job advertising," he said.
Job advertisements declined in every state with the largest falls recorded in Western Australia and Victoria.
Official employment data for July are due on Thursday.
